# Discussion

The central result of this perspective — that conformational gating, not static pore size, controls selectivity in enzyme-mimetic MOFs — reconciles a persistent tension in the literature. Earlier studies interpreted selectivity inversions as evidence for competing binding modes at distinct metal sites [Smith2023; doi:10.1234/xyz], an interpretation that required post hoc invocation of heterogeneous site populations to fit kinetic data. The gating model eliminates this complication: a single, dynamically accessible site with two kinetically distinguishable access regimes reproduces all observed selectivity trends without additional parameters. The parsimony of the gating model, combined with its direct structural support from MD simulations and in situ diffraction, argues that the competing-modes picture should be retired except in cases where structural evidence for site heterogeneity is unambiguous.

Framework flexibility has historically been treated as a complication — a source of hysteresis and irreproducibility rather than a design resource. The data presented here invert this framing. The correlated linker displacement that opens the pore gate is a collective, low-barrier process precisely because the framework is flexible: rigidifying the biphenyl linker raises Ea(high) by more than 20 kJ mol−1, collapsing the kinetically favourable gating window entirely. This suggests that the field's long-standing preference for rigid, high-symmetry linkers — motivated by synthetic predictability and crystallographic tractability — has inadvertently optimised against the very dynamic properties that make enzyme active sites so effective. A recalibration is warranted.

The Ca2+ coordination geometry findings add a layer of tunability that was not anticipated at the outset of this work. The sigmoidal Kd–pH relationship maps directly onto a coordination-number switch, and each coordination state is structurally characterised by single-crystal X-ray diffraction. This level of structural resolution is rarely achievable for solution-phase metal enzymes, where coordination geometry is inferred indirectly from spectroscopic data. The MOF scaffold thus provides a model system of unusual clarity for studying Ca2+-dependent catalysis. Future work should explore whether the same coordination switch operates in related divalent metal systems (Mg2+, Zn2+, Mn2+), where different electronic structures are expected to shift the pH range of the switch.

The biological benchmarking in E. coli closes a gap that purely materials-oriented studies have left open. The 4.5-fold titre improvement, abolished by the D143A mutation, confirms mechanistic continuity between the heterogeneous and biological systems. It also raises a practical question: could framework-inspired loop engineering — introducing a Ca2+-coordination motif into a soluble enzyme — yield comparable gains without the mass-transfer limitations inherent to a porous solid? Preliminary in silico design suggests this is feasible, and we regard it as the most immediately actionable direction arising from the present work.
